# `⌷` — Index

`I⌷Y` indexes `Y`. The left argument has one item for each leading axis of `Y`. Axes that it omits are taken whole. `⌷Y` is identity. After an array, [Dot](dot.qmd) indexing writes the same selection: `x.(I)` is `(I)⌷x`.

```apl
m←3 4⍴⍳12
2⌷m                ⍝ 5 6 7 8
2 3⌷m              ⍝ 7
```

Each item of the left argument is a single position, an array of positions, or `∞`. A single position removes its axis from the result. An array of positions replaces the axis with its own shape. Enclose an array of positions for one axis, because a plain vector gives one position for each axis.

```apl
v←10 20 30
[3 1]⌷v            ⍝ 30 10
m←3 4⍴⍳12
(2 3)(1 4)⌷m       ⍝ [5 8 ⋄ 9 12]
```

Positions count from 1. Negative positions count from the end, so `¯1` is the last position.

```apl
v←10 20 30
¯1⌷v               ⍝ 30
[¯1 1]⌷v           ⍝ 30 10
```

An array of positions whose elements are vectors does choose indexing. Each vector is one coordinate, with one position for each axis of `Y`.

```apl
m←3 4⍴⍳12
[(1 2)(3 ¯1)]⌷m    ⍝ 2 12
```

`∞` takes a whole axis, and `¯∞` takes it in reverse order. They are valid only as a whole item, not inside an array of positions.

```apl
m←3 4⍴⍳12
∞ 2⌷m              ⍝ 2 6 10
¯∞ ∞⌷m             ⍝ ⊖3 4⍴⍳12
```

On a keyed axis, a string is one key.

```apl
T←"aa" "bb":1 2
"bb"⌷T             ⍝ 2
```

Assignment through `⌷` replaces the selected items. A missing key is added, even on an axis with no keys.

```apl
x←10 20 30
(¯1⌷x)←9
x                  ⍝ 10 20 9
T←"aa" "bb":1 2
("cc"⌷T)←3
T                  ⍝ "aa" "bb" "cc":1 2 3
```

With an axis, `⌷⍤[K]` applies the left argument's items to the axes `K`.

```apl
2⌷⍤[2]3 4⍴⍳12       ⍝ 2 6 10
```

## Errors

- `RANK`: left argument not a scalar or vector
- `LENGTH`: more items than axes
- `INDEX`: position 0, position outside its axis, missing key
- `DOMAIN`: non-integral position, `∞` or `¯∞` inside an array of positions
